newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - China lauds Mao 20 years after death.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - China lauds Mao 20 years after death.

text.p: China's breakneck development and a vigorous new consumer culture may have steamrollered Mao Zedong's political and economic legacy, but at least the library of the late revolutionary leader is in safe hands.

China's diligent archivists -- part of an intellectual class once reviled by Maoist cultural commissars -- have gathered 90,000 books kept by the "Great Helmsman", along with 30,000 of his papers and documents, for posterity.
Manuscripts are not the only Mao mementos still enthusiastically collected by a society that appears as keen to celebrate his cult as it is to bury his policies.

Two decades after his death, theme restaurants serving Mao's favourite dishes pull in crowds of diners and a popular appetite for Mao-associated retro-kitsch has spawned a small private sector industry that would have infuriated the devout Marxist.
In the countryside, farmers in some areas prostrate themselves before Mao effigies in temple rituals that the revolutionary leader would have condemned as feudal superstition.

At a Saturday concert to mark the anniversary of Mao's death on September 9, 1976, performers stuck to such politically correct classics as "Chairman Mao's Kindness and Grace Are Higher Than Mountains, Longer Than Rivers" -- but sang them clad in silk ties and slit dresses unthinkable under his puritan social rule.
Listeners said Mao still had a role to play even in a China where the market rules over communist central planning and social uniformity is a distant memory.
"China is developing and slowly growing stronger...but there is still a feeling that we need that kind of Mao spirit," said one member of the audience, teacher Li Qingshen.
Another listener who came with a party of trainee government officials agreed, saying: "It's good for the students to learn about the spirit of those days."

The respect Mao still commands in China can seem bizarre in the light of his policy disasters, such as the 1958 launch of the Great Leap Forward campaign that caused the death through starvation of tens of millions and the 1966-76 ultra-leftist Cultural Revolution that plunged China into turmoil.
Supporters say Mao's mistakes must be measured against his achievement in uniting China and making it a world power again after centuries of decline.
After the chairman's death, the cult of his personality declined -- only to boom anew in recent years.
But while Chinese angry at growing corruption, new inequality and social instability often pepper their complaints with references to the Mao years, few say they want to turn back the clock.
For those who have prospered under the market-style reforms that have replaced Mao's Stalinist approach to economics, honouring the chairman appears mainly a matter of nostalgia.

The winding down of Mao's state-sponsored personality cult, and its replacement with an official line that acknowledges his failings as well as his strengths, have left individuals more room to take personal stock of his legacy.
"To commemorate Mao is to commemorate his spirit," said Yuan Xiaoji, a 41-year-old private businessman. "It absolutely does not mean we want a return to his policies."
Zhang Lijia, author of a book on Western impressions of Mao -- a work that ran afoul of censors who still jealously guard his memory -- said: "In China there is now more diversity of views about Mao.
"In the countryside many people still love and respect him...city folks are different, more critical and questioning."
Simple nostalgia was a major driving force behind the resurgent popularity of Mao memorabilia and the revival of the revolutionary songs, ballets and shows associated with his rule, she said.

While song titles like "Chairman Mao's Warriors Listen Closest to the Party" can seem clumsy to foreign ears, some good tunes were another force behind the Mao revival, anniversary concert-goers said.
"Mao was a great leader," said one audience member, humming happily to himself after the show. "I really like these songs."
